contrasts.title: ship / sheep
contrasts.tip: /ɪ/ is short and relaxed: the tongue is low and the lips hardly stretch. It is between the 'i' and the 'e' of Spanish. /iː/ is long and tense, like a long Spanish 'i' with the lips stretched. A common mistake is using the Spanish 'i' for both, so 'ship' sounds like 'sheep'.

contrasts.title: cat / cut
contrasts.tip: /æ/ is made with the jaw low and the mouth open. It sounds between 'a' and 'e'. /ʌ/ is short, relaxed and central, with the mouth almost closed, like a very soft 'a'. A common mistake is saying the Spanish 'a' for both, so 'cat' and 'cut' sound the same.

contrasts.title: bad / bed
contrasts.tip: /ɛ/ is similar to the Spanish 'e' in 'perro'. /æ/ is more open: lower the jaw and stretch the lips a little, as if you were saying 'a' and 'e' at the same time. A common mistake is saying 'e' for both, so 'bad' sounds like 'bed'.

contrasts.title: cot / cut
contrasts.tip: /ɑ/ is a long, open 'a' made at the back of the mouth, with the lips not rounded. /ʌ/ is short, relaxed and with the mouth more closed. A common mistake is using the Spanish 'a' for both, so 'cot' and 'cut' sound the same.

contrasts.title: full / fool
contrasts.tip: /ʊ/ is short and relaxed, with the lips barely rounded. /uː/ is long and tense, with the lips very rounded and pushed forward. A common mistake is using the Spanish 'u' for both, so 'full' sounds like 'fool'.

contrasts.title: berry / very
contrasts.tip: For /b/ you press both lips together. For /v/ you touch your top teeth to your bottom lip and let the air vibrate. In Spanish 'b' and 'v' sound the same, so speakers often say /b/ both times, and 'very' sounds like 'berry'.

contrasts.title: bus / buzz
contrasts.tip: /s/ is a voiceless hiss. /z/ is the same hiss with voice in your throat (touch your neck to feel it). Mexican Spanish has no /z/ sound, so people tend to say /s/, and 'buzz' or 'rise' sound like 'bus' or 'rice'.

contrasts.title: three / tree
contrasts.tip: For /θ/ put the tip of your tongue between your teeth and blow softly. For /t/ touch the top gum and release the air suddenly. Mexican Spanish has no /θ/, so people replace it with /t/ (or /s/), and 'three' sounds like 'tree'.

contrasts.title: think / sink
contrasts.tip: /θ/ is made with the tongue between the teeth and a soft breath. /s/ is made with the tongue behind the teeth. In Mexican Spanish 'z' and 'c' sound like /s/, so it is very common to replace /θ/ with /s/, and 'think' sounds like 'sink'.

contrasts.title: they / day
contrasts.tip: /ð/ is voiced: put your tongue between your teeth and make your voice vibrate, like the soft 'd' in 'nada' but at the start of a word. /d/ is a firm stop with the tongue on the gum. A common mistake is using /d/ at the start of a word, so 'they' sounds like 'day'.

contrasts.title: shoe / chew
contrasts.tip: /ʃ/ is a continuous sound, like saying 'shhh' to ask for quiet, with no tongue closure. /tʃ/ is the Spanish 'ch': you close first and then release the air. A common mistake is saying 'ch' instead of 'sh', so 'shoe' sounds like 'chew'.

contrasts.title: jet / yet
contrasts.tip: /dʒ/ starts with the tongue closing against the roof of the mouth and then releases with friction (like a voiced 'ch'). /j/ has no closure: it is like the 'i' in 'hielo' used as a consonant. Many Spanish speakers say 'y' as /dʒ/ or the other way round, so 'yet' and 'jet' get mixed up.

contrasts.title: cart / card
contrasts.tip: At the end of a word, /d/ is voiced and /t/ is voiceless, but the clearest clue is that the vowel before /d/ is longer ('card') and shorter before /t/ ('cart'). In Spanish, the final 'd' almost disappears, so people tend to say /t/ or drop it. Make the vowel longer and keep your voice going to the end for /d/.

contrasts.title: team / teen
contrasts.tip: For /m/ close your lips; for /n/ keep your lips open and touch the tip of your tongue to the gum. In Spanish, final 'm' and 'n' tend to merge, so 'team' and 'teen' can sound the same. Really close your lips for /m/ and do not close them for /n/.

contrasts.title: pin / pen
contrasts.tip: /ɪ/ is short and relaxed, between the Spanish 'i' and 'e'. /ɛ/ is like the Spanish 'e' in 'perro'. Spanish speakers often say a full Spanish 'i' for /ɪ/, so 'pin' and 'pen' get mixed up. Keep /ɪ/ short and lazy.

contrasts.title: late / let
contrasts.tip: /eɪ/ is a glide: start at 'e' and move towards 'i' (like 'ey' in Spanish 'rey'). /ɛ/ is one short sound with no glide. If you don't glide, 'late' sounds like 'let'.

contrasts.title: not / note
contrasts.tip: /ɑ/ is an open 'a' made at the back of the mouth (American 'not'). /oʊ/ is a glide from 'o' to 'u', with the lips rounding at the end. Spanish speakers often say a Spanish 'o' for both, so 'not' sounds like 'note'.

contrasts.title: caught / coat
contrasts.tip: /ɔ/ is an open 'o' with the jaw low and no glide. /oʊ/ starts at 'o' and moves to 'u' with rounded lips. Use the glide only in /oʊ/: 'coat', 'boat', 'low'.

contrasts.title: she / see
contrasts.tip: /ʃ/ is 'shhh' with rounded lips and the tongue a little back. /s/ is a thin hiss with the tongue behind the teeth. Spanish has no /ʃ/, so 'she' often becomes 'see' and 'ship' becomes 'sip'.

contrasts.title: fan / van
contrasts.tip: For both, the top teeth touch the bottom lip. /f/ is only air; /v/ adds voice (your lip buzzes). Spanish speakers often say /b/ or /f/ instead of /v/, so 'van' sounds like 'ban' or 'fan'.

contrasts.title: bet / but
contrasts.tip: /ɛ/ is like the Spanish 'e'. /ʌ/ is a short, relaxed sound in the middle of the mouth, close to a soft Spanish 'a'. Keep the jaw relaxed for /ʌ/: 'but', 'cup', 'luck'.
